items.body: Listening to Crude Walnut Taste, it is tempting to focus on Giorgi Koberidze‘s compositional rigour: the electroacoustic transformations, the dialogue with Western classical forms, the microscopic attention paid to the behaviour of sound. Those elements are certainly there, but they risk obscuring something equally important. This is a remarkably funny album. After all, the opening track, “Horsing Around”, gives the game away immediately. Crude Walnut Taste is not funny in the sense of parody or quotation, but in the pleasure it takes in constantly wrong-footing the listener who might be expecting an academic work. A gesture suddenly changes direction, a rhythmic idea gathers momentum before being interrupted by an entirely different line of thought. Titles such as “Quasi Sonata-Allegro”, “Experimental, electro-accoustic, spatial audio, Georgian, sound design, Tbilisi, ambient – Adagio” and “Tbilisian Faux-Valse” gesture towards familiar classical forms, but only long enough for Koberidze to dismantle them. As the composer explains in the accompanying interview, these references belong to an earlier period of his practice, when his relationship with classical composition was more direct and, in his own words, more “primitive”. And this is the paradox at the heart of the album. On the one hand it sounds almost primitive, built from raw acoustic matter; on the other, the speed with which ideas appear, collide and disappear constantly propels it forward. Without resorting to the tired label of “retro-futurism”, the image that kept returning while I listened was Georgiy Daneliya’s Kin-dza-dza!. The 1986 Soviet science-fiction comedy follows two ordinary citizens transported to a distant galaxy where advanced civilisation appears to have regressed into something primitive. The film was, of course, scored by the late Georgian composer Giya Kancheli, yet there is a comparable measure of irony and lightness of touch running through both works. That playfulness extends to the sound world itself. Much of the album is constructed from recordings of the doli, the Georgian drum, chosen precisely because it carries no melodic baggage. Rather than treating the instrument as a symbol of national identity, Koberidze breaks it down into tiny fragments that become the raw material for an unexpectedly broad range of textures. The result is music that remains unmistakably physical. Even the electronics rarely transform those sounds outright. However, what remains most surprising, is the album’s speed, and not just its manic kinetic energy, but also the speed with which ideas appear only to mutate. Very little is allowed to settle. Musical thoughts collide with a kind of controlled frenzy that recalls someone thinking faster than they can speak. And yet, despite this restless surface, the music never feels erratic. It remains playful without becoming flippant, rigorous without turning solemn. That is a rare balance, and one that gives Crude Walnut Taste its distinctive character. To help us crack the walnut, we approached Giorgi Koberidze directly. Crude Walnut Taste began life as a 20-channel spatial work commissioned for MONOM’s 4D Sound system before being reimagined in stereo for this release. How did the process of translating such a physically immersive piece into a two-channel format affect your relationship to the material? Were there aspects of the original spatial architecture that had to be sacrificed, or did the reduction reveal new details that were previously hidden? I actually already knew how the piece would sound in stereo, because I don’t have a twenty-channel speaker setup at my studio. So while working on it, I was composing in stereo from the start, imagining what sound could fit where. We then spent two weeks at MONOM Studio in Berlin, where we had the chance to rearrange the piece, add things, and sometimes exclude things, but the core idea of the music was already written in stereo, and that’s what made it possible to translate the twenty-channel piece back down. Of course, a lot is lost in that reduction, but the core idea is still there. It works almost the same as watching an IMAX film in a normal movie theatre: whatever really matters stays in focus, stays at the centre. What the IMAX size gives you additionally is maybe more air, more space, something that isn’t crucial to understanding the film itself. I’d say it’s the same with this piece: what really matters is still there in stereo. The MONOM system just gives more space and some additional ideas, but I wouldn’t say the piece is focused only on those twenty channels. Generally, my belief is that good music can be played on a single-string guitar, even if it was written for a hundred-channel system, as long as the idea itself is strong, and as long as the music matters more than the form. If we’re not talking about a piece where form is more important than the music, then I think it’s easily translatable anywhere. Across Forests, Tales, Cities, Forests, its Epilogue, and now Crude Walnut Taste, the doli seems to occupy an increasingly central role in your work. On this album, the instrument is extensively sampled, dissected and reconstructed through micro-editing techniques. What drew you to the doli as the primary sonic source, and how did transforming it electronically alter your perception of an instrument so deeply embedded in Georgian musical culture? I use the doli because it has no pitch. My problem with using tonal instruments from the Caucasus – the duduk, say, or the chuniri – is that they come with already-written melodies and harmonies, and I find it very hard to know how to use that material in modern music. At some point I decided I would never touch existing melody or harmony, because it’s already there, it’s already enough. It doesn’t need anything from me, or from anyone, to be transformed. The doli is interesting because you can use it without ever touching a melody or a harmony, it gives you a lot of possibility to take micro-material from it instead. But anyone who understands sound and sound design knows that, basically, you can turn any sound into anything. The instrument you choose is just a source for material, and from there you can go anywhere; it’s really about what physical material you’re comfortable working with. In my case, it’s the doli simply because it’s here – you’re in Georgia, there are dolis everywhere, you can just grab one. Also, the quality of that sound already carries something very familiar to every Georgian. By using it, you’re lightly touching this historical heritage, but it doesn’t give you licence to overuse it – to base your music on something already precious to Georgians and then claim it as your own. Some people use old melodies, traditional melodies especially, and I’m not against using old pop music in modern work. But when it comes to traditional music, it’s more delicate. So even when we do use tonal instruments like the duduk, we’re very careful never to cross into an already-written melody from Georgian folk music. Earlier works such as Forests, Tales, Cities, Forests felt almost cartographic, mapping landscapes, memories and imagined geographies through graphic scores, ensembles and field recordings. Crude Walnut Taste seems more focused on texture, gesture and acoustic matter itself. Do you see this album as a departure from those narrative and spatial concerns, or as another way of exploring the relationship between place, memory and sound? Also, several track titles—”Tbilisian Faux-Valse”, “Quasi Sonata-Allegro”, “Experimental, electro-accoustic, spatial audio, Georgian, sound design, Tbilisi, ambient – Adagio”—appear to reference established musical forms, yet the music itself constantly undermines expectations through fragmentation, electroacoustic processing and playful subversion. To what extent are these titles intended as affectionate dialogues with classical traditions, and how important is humour or irony within your compositional practice? First, some context: Crude Walnut Taste was actually written much earlier than Forests, Tales, Cities, Forests – about five years earlier. What the two albums share is a certain playfulness with, and closeness to, classical music. In 2019, when I wrote Crude Walnut Taste, I was a much younger student of classical composition, so the way I integrated that knowledge into the album was more direct, less hidden, even a bit more “primitive” – the melodic and harmonic moments lean more overtly classical. That’s also where the track titles come from, which I actually chose later, closer to the album’s release: names like “Tbilisian Faux-Valse” or “Quasi Sonata-Allegro.” They’re not literal sonata-allegros or waltzes, of course, but the mood and the harmonic gestures really are drawn from there. Looking back, I wouldn’t use these references so directly today – in Forests, Tales, Cities, Forests, similar techniques are used much more hidden, on a deeper, more background level. So, from that perspective, this earlier album carries a bit of irony, a bit of humour, and that’s something I’m quite fond of. I’ve always wanted to find a way to put humour inside music – it’s genuinely hard to do. My friend and musical collaborator Luka, the other half of Awwwaea, always used to come up with wonderfully funny musical ideas; I was constantly amazed at how he could make our whole friend group laugh for hours over a single musical idea. I’d say this album carries a little of that same spirit. At the same time, it’s a very personal record. Even the title comes from childhood: crude walnut taste refers to eating very raw, unripe walnuts as kids – cracking them open with your fingers while they’re still green, watching your fingers turn green and then black from the juice. That taste takes me straight back to those childhood memories: sometimes fast, sometimes a little sad, but mostly very bright, full of colourful images and imagination – but still raw, because the sounds themselves are raw. After I finished the album, a friend told me at a small concert that it felt like “music made for sounds no one else is using.” I loved that description, because the sounds you hear really are raw – almost taken straight from the computer as they are, with very little additional sound design or processing layered on top. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以格鲁吉亚传统鼓doli为核心素材，但并非将其作为民族象征，而是将其拆解为微小碎片，作为电声音响的原始材料。作曲家科贝里泽频繁将古典形式作为引子随即拆解，类似伪奏鸣曲、伪圆舞曲的标题暗示了对学院传统的戏谑姿态。专辑充满快速变换的音乐思绪，控制下的狂热中保持着精确的幽默感。声响层面，电子处理克制地保留物理感，电声变换与西方古典形式形成对话。评论将其与苏联电影《基甸扎之星球》的讽刺与轻盈气质相比较，凸显出一种原始与高度精密并存的悖论美学。电声技术、格鲁吉亚传统打击乐与当代作曲思维的融合，使作品在跨界语境中展现出独特的艺术视角。

items.body: Multiple active listens never feel like a chore, and are instantly rewarded by the lavishness of the sounds and the cleverness of the compositions, bringing together awe, humor, and bewilderment. And what else can we ask of experimental music? This aesthetic of contrast between composite lumps of sound and silence Der Saal tobt by Ervin Omsk   From Switched-On Bach to countless orchestral sound libraries promising to be hyper realistic, the history of electronic music’s mimicry of and liaison with classical spans over half a century. Most of the time, this relationship has manifested in two clear-cut ways: imitation and reinterpretation. A frequent intention is to make electronics act like the expansive (and expensive) organ of the orchestra or chamber ensemble, trying to sound as close as possible to the “real thing,” such as in a lot of pop music and soundtracks; but on the other (more intriguing) hand, electronic composers have also looked back at classical to reinterpret it through new technologies and sensibilities: the aforementioned 1968 study of baroque on the Moog synthesizer by Wendy Carlos, or Tomita’s Snowflakes Are Dancing (1974) performing the impressionistic romanticism of Debussy, all the way to recent takes on minimalism such as Erik Hall’s half-acoustic-half-electronic recreations or, to take it to the extreme and to a more underground angle, composermodel’s MF18M, an excellent all-midi, trance-infused rendition of Steve Reich‘s Music for 18 Musicians. A glaringly underrepresented style however is the manic use of the orchestra in works such as Luciano Berio’s 1969 Sinfonia, or Pierre Boulez’s Dérive 1 (1984), or what one might call the the final boss in this most-chaotic “genre,” Karleinz Stockhausen’s Gruppen (1955-57), for three orchestras (yes, three). Save for some pieces (like the title track), Ervin Omsk’s latest Der Saal tobt’(“The Hall in uproar”) is closer to these works than to, say, an extreme decomposition of club music. The opening track, “Memo Grisaille,” makes it instantly clear: isolated clusters of sound straddling between strings, brass, and pure electric glitches come and give way to silence, before they start interacting in a complex and wider tapestry of sounds. This aesthetic of contrast between composite lumps of sound and silence recurs throughout Der Saal tobt, and the whitespace makes each sonic assault all the more flavorful. Every pseudo-instrument is crafted to be as full and satisfying a sound as possible: in “Echt jetzt” (“seriously…?”) hyper-speed delays make each percussive atom resonate more like held notes than bells or beats. When actual long-held synths do appear, like in the following “Greller Block” or in “Offenes Feld” (“Garish Block” and “Open Field” – maybe opposites?) the drones still appear unstable, as if they were about to implode and, after a second of tension, explode back into shards of colour. Which happens in between tracks anyway. A simple industrial piece to a positively jarring experience :: Interestingly, the title track (and single) of the album is somewhat of a different affair. It is probably the only piece with a clear rhythm–if syncopated to excess–played by airy synths with tones bending sharply like glissandos rather than drum samples. This attention to original sound design turns the rhythm from what could have been a simple industrial piece to a positively jarring experience: why am I nodding along to this? How come my body recognizes the pace? This more rhythmic approach comes back in “Nicht senden doch senden” (“do not send send anyway”), mixed in with everything else, from the glitchy delays to the bent pitches, before the closer “Beim besten Willen” (“with the best will in the world”) harkens back to the opener and to XX century atonality with the full-on orchestral stirring bringing the record to a full circle. It’s hard to find any obvious point of comparison in contemporary electronic music, if not maybe some of Nathan Ho’s serialist work or Rashad Becker’s Traditional Music of Notional Species; but where Becker’s “Dances” and “Themes” sounded like linguistic attempts at communication from an alien civilisation, Ervin Omsk’s compositions are impressionistic and expressionistic, conveying a much more holistic content. While the first reaction to an album like this could very well be “how the hell was this made,” especially for someone who dabbles in making experimental music–the press release mentions manipulated recordings of an alto recorder and pure synthesis, but there just must be more!–something that distinguishes Der Saal tobt from a lot of technical or academic-leaning avant-garde electronics is its allure, and the persuasiveness with which it leads the listener further in. Multiple active listens never feel like a chore, and are instantly rewarded by the lavishness of the sounds and the cleverness of the compositions, bringing together awe, humor, and bewilderment. And what else can we ask of experimental music? Der Saal tobt is available on Orange Milk. [Bandcamp] Der Saal tobt by Ervin OmskThe post Ervin Omsk :: Der Saal tobt (Orange Milk) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑将电子音乐与管弦乐语汇进行深度的解构与重构，延续了从Wendy Carlos到Tomita以来电子音乐对古典的再诠释传统，但更接近Berio、Boulez和Stockhausen所代表的混乱与密集编排美学。Ervin Omsk以孤立的声音集群为起点，让弦乐、铜管般的质感与电子毛刺相互交织，在长段沉默与突发性声响洪流之间反复切换，形成极强的张力对比。合成器被刻意处理成不稳定的状态：延迟让打击乐原子延展为持续音，持续低音则随时可能崩塌为彩色碎片。每一轨伪乐器音色都被雕琢得饱满厚实，既有古典配器的庄重外壳，又充满实验电子的偶然性与拼贴感。Orange Milk厂牌的地下实验定位与专辑的激进美学高度契合，是当代电子-古典融合领域中一次颇具野心的探索。

items.body: By the third instalment of their Is Noise series, TAKAAT [pronounced tuh-cot and meaning “noise” in the Tuareg language Tamashek] have moved further from the raw collision of Tuareg guitar and punk that initially defined the project. The trio has become a duo here, without Souleymane Ibrahim’s live drums or any vocals. Vol. 3 is more exploratory and searching, less concerned with songs than with seeing how far Ahmoudou Madassane and Mikey Coltun can stretch their shared musical language. Drum machines, drones and field recordings move into the space left behind. The four-part Ijit N’elwan begins almost by withholding TAKAAT altogether. “Ijit N’elwan 1” opens with field recordings and remains a brief, ambient introduction, establishing a sense of place before amplification takes over. The second part strips things down to an extended, heavily distorted guitar passage whose sustained tones eventually push the track into drone territory. “Ijit N’elwan 3” initially reveals something bluesier in Madassane’s playing, but gradually acquires greater weight and distortion as it progresses, while the final part heads somewhere more psychedelic. Coltun’s comments in the accompanying interview help explain why this expansion feels natural. He draws a connection between the trance-like repetition at the heart of Tuareg guitar music and drone, as well as between the distortion of contemporary Takamba—music blasted through overloaded radios and megaphone speakers—and the punk, noise and experimental music that shaped his own listening. On Vol. 3, those affinities no longer need to be announced: they have become part of the music’s vocabulary. There is also a deliberate sense of risk. Each new TAKAAT EP enters a different world while remaining recognisably part of the same universe, and Vol. 3 takes that idea further than its predecessors. The duo format makes the music feel simultaneously more exposed and more open-ended as well as restless and unafraid of charting new territory. To make sense of the noise we reached out directly to TAKAAT with Mikey Coltun answering our questions. Across the three Is Noise volumes, TAKAAT has moved quite quickly from the raw Tuareg guitar and punk energy of Vol. 1, through the live-to-tape Tinariwen reworkings of Vol. 2, to the drones, drum machines, field recordings and much denser noise of Vol. 3. Was this evolution something you imagined when TAKAAT began, or has each volume simply opened up possibilities for the next one? Mikey Coltun: It’s been a mix of both. We knew there was a lot to explore sonically when Ahmoudou and I started the band but to what extent was a bit more unknown until we started touring and experimenting both live and during the recording process. Each Is Noise is recorded to tape. That’s kinda the overall concept. Similarly if you look at the album art (shout out to our designer Can Misirlioglu) throughout the volumes the structure remains the same but is a different perspective and zoomed out throughout each volume. This was intentional from the beginning as it relates to the music and the progression of each Is Noise volume. Mikey, you’ve drawn a connection between the distortion of modern Takamba—particularly the tehardent amplified through blown-out radios—and the noise and experimental music you grew up with in Washington, D.C. [Andy Downing, Matter News, 4 March 2026]. On Vol. 3, do those traditions actually meet in the way you make sound, or are they still distinct references that you bring into TAKAAT from different directions? Mikey Coltun: There’s definitely all of those influences – Takamba, punk, noise and experimental music present on Vol. 3. Similar to later era John Coltrane, a lot of Tuareg music is drone music at its core. With Tuareg guitar music, a simple chord structure with trance-like rhythms and melodies often played for long periods of time is no different than the spirituality of drone music and this is something Ahmoudou and I were interested in exploring. Taking our guitar and bass and blasting it through amps creating different sonic distortions can be also heard when seeing Takamba music live but instead of the guitar amps you have a blown out radio receiver roaring through megaphone speakers. As Ahmoudou has put it, TAKAAT is the “feeling of being in the desert at night.” Vol. 3 also changes the basic instrumental architecture of TAKAAT: drum machines, drone synths and manipulated field recordings become central alongside Ahmoudou’s guitar and Mikey’s bass. What interested you about moving away from the more recognisable guitar/bass/drums setup of the earlier volumes, and how did that change the way you approached improvisation? Mikey Coltun: It’s important for Ahmoudou and I to be experimenting musically and taking risks. We talk a lot about how Taureg legends Tinariwen pushed, what Tuareg music is, and what we’re doing with TAKAAT is breaking the expectations of the known Tuareg rock sound. We want each record to push into a different world while still staying in the universe of TAKAAT. This goes the same with our shows. Each tour Ahmoudou and I want to present something different with TAKAAT. The first few tours we did the trio, last tour was a duo presenting a loud drone and blown out drum machines, and next tour will be something different too. We’re taking risks and we want people to come take these risks with us. This is the only way to push out of comfort zones and create something new. You’ve described the trust developed through eight years of playing together as something that allows TAKAAT to take risks, while Mikey has also spoken about the project as a return to a more DIY world where there is less pressure to perform in a particular way [Andy Downing, Matter News, 4 March 2026]. Does TAKAAT give you a kind of freedom that you don’t necessarily have in Mdou Moctar—and has that freedom changed the way you listen and respond to one another when you play? Mikey Coltun: It was really clear early on touring together with Mdou Moctar that Ahmoudou and I were excited by similar music. I brought a lot of different types of bands on tour with Mdou. All of the music is by groups and artists that I love. While some of the groups could have been challenging to listeners it was important to me to draw that connection with what we were doing with Mdou. Mdou’s music was different and challenging to some in the Tuareg wedding scene in Agadez, Niger. With a lot of these bands I brought on tour I found Ahmoudou’s interest peaked. Whenever there was an opportunity on tour I would take him to see sound installations, free jazz groups, modern art, etc… and he really does appreciate that. Because Ahmoudou and I have similar interests sonically, there is a lot of trust and comfortability to experiment and try new things together with TAKAAT. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items._cn_summary: TAKAAT的《Is Noise》第三卷从图阿雷格吉他与朋克的原始碰撞转向更为探索性的二人组编制。Ahmoudou Madassane与Mikey Coltun放弃了现场鼓和人声，引入鼓机、无人机音调和田野录音，将音乐语言推向更极端的实验领域。专辑的四部分《Ijit N'elwan》以环境声音开场，逐步进入失真吉他的持续音与厚重的噪声层，融合了图阿雷格音乐的迷幻重复性与当代Takamba通过过载收音机和扩音器播放所产生的失真质感。每一卷都以录音至磁带为概念，专辑封面亦延续统一视觉语言，呈现出在熟悉的音乐宇宙内不断冒险拓展边界的创作态度。

items.body: Da Punch is the fourth album from the Parisian project Krystal System. ‘Bonnie’ and ‘N°7’ are joined by a new member, bassist ‘Phi’, who had already appeared on the EP preceding the album. Remarkably, this is their first full-length release since 2013. On ‘Da Punch’, Krystal System takes a critical look at society and interpersonal relationships, resulting in a collection of 13 tracks. I’ve always had a soft spot for Krystal System because, to me, they sound like a big ‘f*** you’ to all those bands that simply keep repeating themselves, gradually getting lost in a lack of creativity. Krystal System continues along its established path, delivering uncompromising compositions that blend guitar and electronics into an Electro-Post-Punk sound, driven by Bonnie’s passionate vocals. She sometimes sings in her native French, but most of the tracks are performed in English, delivered with that unmistakable and rather sexy French accent. N°7 also takes the microphone, providing a nice counterbalance to the female vocals and occasionally resulting in a duet. The songs are varied and, as mentioned, uncompromising. Their cover of Front 242’s “Headhunter” is a great example. Rather than simply copying the original—which would be sacrilege—they give it their own interpretation, and it really works. There are other, even stronger tracks to discover, with Krystal System occasionally channelling Rammstein-like guitar riffs and Depeche Mode-style melodies, while still remaining firmly rooted in their own sound. That’s what I call a modern Punk attitude, and it really appeals to me. Krystal System will need to put themselves back on the map for a wider audience, but music lovers who already know the band will simply be delighted to see them return with such a cool album. (Rating:8). Listen to “A World That Is Yours”: A World That Is Yours by Krystal System About Krystal System Krystal System started in Paris, France, in April 2006 under the name Krystal. The founding duo was Bonnie on vocals and guitar and N°7 (also stylized as Seven) on vocals, synths, and programming. A first demo, “Demain n’existe pas,” came before the project gained early exposure through the 2007 International Cravefest Video Awards and concerts in France and Switzerland. Around 2007 the duo signed to Belgian label Alfa Matrix and adopted the name Krystal System. Their debut album, “Underground,” followed on November 14, 2008, then the seven-track EP “Underground: VooDoo Night Sessions” on November 27, 2009, “Nuclear” on June 17, 2011, and “Rage” on March 15, 2013. Krystal System returned in 2025 with the “Éclats Rouges” EP, its first studio release since “Rage” and its first with bassist φ (Phi), expanding the lineup to a trio. “Da Punch,” the fourth Krystal System album, followed on June 26, 2026, again with the trio of Bonnie, N°7, and Phi. The 13-track release was made available digitally via Bandcamp and on CD through the Alfa Matrix Store, whose edition adds two bonus tracks, “Newclear Winter” and a 2025 version of the track. The album also includes a cover of a Front 242 song, “Headhunter.”
items._cn_summary: 巴黎三人乐队Krystal System暌违多年推出的第四张专辑《Da Punch》，以13首作品延续其不妥协的电子后朋克路线，将吉他与电子音色交织融合，核心驱动来自主唱Bonnie充满激情的演唱，辅以法语与英语交替呈现，后者带有独特的法语口音。乐队成员N°7同样担任主唱，与Bonnie形成对唱平衡。专辑包含对Front 242经典曲目《Headhunter》的重新演绎，并非简单复刻，而是融入自身风格的成功改编。整体创作在保留乐队自身辨识度的同时，吸收了Rammstein式吉他riff与Depeche Mode式旋律线条，体现出对当下社会的批判视角。专辑以数字与CD两种形式由比利时小众厂牌Alfa Matrix发行，CD版额外收录两首加曲。

items.body: Bracaloni’s latest traverse moves through warm, spacious soundscapes built for getting lost within, where atmosphere lingers long after each piece fades. A surreal sonic collage of ambient electronics Stars are Crashing, Home are Burning, Hearts are Changing-Notes from a Distant World/Detuned Lullabies for the Old Planet by Fallen   Like a shield of emotive melodic strands gathering before our eyes, Lorenzo Bracaloni’s Fallen project shifts through time and space, blending ethereal voices with instrumental electronica across the long-winded (but apropo) Touched Music title, Stars are Crashing, Homes are Burning, Hearts are Changing-Notes from a Distant World/Detuned Lullabies for the Old Planet. Fifteen slices of life unfold through ambient propulsion, opening with cascading sonic beauty on “Rusted Gardens,” where pitter-patter patterns breathe against a spacious atmosphere, quietly revealing how essential sound can be. Bracaloni’s signature drifts into darker territory with “Violent Winds,” yet remains light and airy, its floating voices drawing us deeper into a mesmerizing current. Downtempo bubbles and understated beatwork provide a gentle respite on “Wide Red Skies.” These are tranquil, ethereal spaces where music opens pathways rather than directing the listener. “The Vanishing,” “Hearts are Changing,” “Chasing Mechanical Butterflies,” and “From Dry Iron Valleys to Utopian Realms” could each have formed the core of a powerful extended player, while closing piece “Direction Home (Ruins Pathway)” ignites something deeper, allowing everything that came before to drift into one surreal sonic collage of ambient electronics, emotional textures, and shifting plateaus. Early heavyweight ambient/IDM artists such as Arovane, Biosphere, and Global Communication, alongside cinematic world-builders like Yagya, Secede, and Deepchord / Echospace, will find familiar connections throughout. As a result, Bracaloni’s latest traverse moves through warm, spacious soundscapes built for getting lost within, where atmosphere lingers long after each piece fades. Stars are Crashing, Homes are Burning, Hearts are Changing-Notes from a Distant World/Detuned Lullabies for the Old Planet is available on Touched Music. items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由Lorenzo Bracaloni的Fallen项目在Touched Music厂牌发行，收录十五首作品，以环境电子为核心构建出温暖而空旷的声场。整体手法偏向氛围推进而非旋律主导，开篇的"Rusted Gardens"以细碎的音色颗粒在宽阔空间中铺陈，"Violent Winds"转向更幽暗的氛围但仍保持轻盈漂浮感，"Wide Red Skies"引入低调的碎拍节拍作为呼吸的间歇。专辑的中段多首曲目如"The Vanishing""Hearts are Changing""Chasing Mechanical Butterflies"各自独立成篇，结尾曲"Direction Home (Ruins Pathway)"将前文的碎片汇聚成一幅完整的超现实声音拼贴。人声采样与器乐电子相互交织，情感纹理层层累积，承袭了Arovane、Biosphere、Global Communication等早期环境/IDM前辈的脉络，同时也与Yagya、Deepchord等电影感世界构建者的审美相通。整张作品不以结构取胜，而是邀请听者在其间迷失，让氛围在音乐消散后仍持续停留。

items.body: Everything about the sound design and palette of Window To Askoy seems suspended in the heat of summer rains and tropical smog. Yet it’s the soulful element that’s paramount: an exquisite melancholy and blessed-out bliss shape the ventricles and vessels of these lean cuts. Exquisite melancholy and blessed-out bliss Zoku – Zoku maintain the altitude of their own exciting frequencies alongside the heights and depths of the frankly awesome Strugatsky Brothers album Window To Askey. Atmosphere is the key ingredient here. There is beauty, tenderness and a sense of wisdom and maturity visible beneath an overt display of technique. The realms created are dub-heavy in tension and color, occasionally recalling Bvdub, but this isn’t intended as a direct comparison. The brothers (Stas Kovalev, aka Keiss) are clearly distinct, yet that fugue-like quality and deftness of hand is apparent throughout. Rain features, reverbs write verbs across low-hung bass, while beats staccato in and out of the visual field being created. Mid-range tension stutters into view only to evaporate moments later. Everything about the sound design and palette seems suspended in the heat of summer rains and tropical smog. Yet it’s the soulful element that’s paramount: an exquisite melancholy and blessed-out bliss shape the ventricles and vessels of these lean cuts. Across ten tracks and three extras, the brothers retain interest and keep expectations poised on the edge of what’s possible next, doing so with rare panache. I might call this ambient, but that would be a lazy get-out. This is experimental electronic music wearing its influences on clean sleeves, facing forward with valor, integrity and just enough—and plenty—of both. Recommended for the ethereal textured moods of FSOL and the abstract dub’n fuzz of Jack Dangers. Window To Askoy is available on Zoku – Zoku. items._cn_summary: 这张专辑聚焦于氛围营造与声音设计的精致打磨，将夏日雨季的潮湿与热带烟雾的朦胧感编织进每一轨作品中。整体采用dub质感的基础节奏与低频贝斯线，配合大量的混响空间处理，营造出兼具忧郁与极乐的复杂情感层次。制作手法上注重张力与色彩的平衡，中频区域间歇性出现后即消散，鼓点以断奏形式进出画面，呈现出碎片化的听觉体验。两位创作者（Stas Kovalev与Keiss）展现出明显的复调思维与娴熟技艺，专辑跨越十首正曲与三首附加曲目，保持了贯穿始终的情绪张力。作品明显受到FSOL的空灵质感与Jack Dangers抽象噪音美学的影响，但并未停留在模仿层面，而是在实验电子的框架内形成了自身的艺术辨识度。

items.body: All in all, an emotionally intoxicating, bizarre yet alluring ghostly-ambient trip, augmented by dark clouds of noisy elements. An emotionally intoxicating, bizarre yet alluring ghostly-ambient trip Lost Myths vol. VII by Lost Myths   Based in Achères, France, Lotophagus Records is an indie label with a real interest in unusual and captivating music, crossing the paths of radical experimentalism and various researches into sound morphologies and advanced or hand-crafted electronic manipulations. I discovered their catalogue a while ago and, to say the least, it is full of intriguing albums covering a large spectrum of electronic music sub-genres. I stopped on this new one first for the originality of the concept brought to the fore. The creative motivation of this album lies behind the discovery of a “born to fail” fantasist electro-acoustic instrumentarium with a curious, if not enigmatic, name: Transdimensional Etheric Resonance Phonoscopium. Without entering into the heavily technical description of this machinery, we can see associations with electro-physical instruments and utopian automatic music forged by acousticians and genuinely crazy inventors of the past, such as J. B. Schalkenbach. The Transdimensional Etheric Resonance Phonoscopium, as suggested by its etymology, seems to combine pseudoscience with metaphysical concerns about aetheric properties of sounds: in brief, a noise-producing machine capable of providing magical effects, surrounded by a surreal-futuristic dimension and appealing electroacoustic fairy-like undulating resonances. It is easy to imagine those charming and Dada-esque musical-technical inventions linked to the fruitful artistic creativity of the early 20th century, notably the challenging and humorous poetical universe of Picabia and, more precisely, the steampunk-before-its-time adventurous imaginary world of Albert Robida. Lost Myths is almost an anonymous and highly secret project, as is the Transdimensional Etheric Resonance Phonoscopium itself. The album starts with an awe-inspiring ghostly beauty built on altered choir sequences and fuzzed-out, almost static droney emotional phrases with a sense of depth, nostalgia, and rumbling darkness. The following tracks oscillate between chilling abstract electronica for bleak tones, hauntological effects, distorted micro-noises, and anomalous industrial-mechanical accidents. All in all, an emotionally intoxicating, bizarre yet alluring ghostly-ambient trip, augmented by dark clouds of noisy elements. Somewhere between the lo-fi sonic explorations of Modelbau, Pedestrian Deposit, and Cremation Anxiety. Lost Myths vol. VII is available on Lotophagus. [Bandcamp] Lost Myths vol. items.body: John Coltrane - Olé (Atlantic, 1961) In the mid-1990s I had just graduated from undergrad with a degree in Journalism and absolutely no idea what to do next. I spent the following summer living in a shared house with five other people about my age, one of whom was a good friend and musical partner in our band called “ Joe Joe the Dog Face Boy. ” We were working, we were playing music, all in all, it was fine even if a bit of a confusing time in life. In the living room of the house, next to my room, was a shelf with a bunch of records on it. The records belonged to my friend, who had just been gifted them by his father. He had placed them on the shelf not knowing what to do with them - I am not sure that he even had a record player at this point, as it was the heyday of CDs afterall. I, however, did have a record player that had been accompanying me all through college and would be my only constant companion for the next twenty years or more, so the records, a rather eclectic mix of music from the 60s and 70s, would end up often on my stereo. This was how I encountered Ol é. Olé , John Coltrane’s last album for the Atlantic label, released in 1961, was recorded with his long-time associates MyCoy Tyner on piano and Elvin Jones on drums, which already likely brings certain harmonic and rhythmic sounds to mind. Joining them was trumpeter Freddie Hubbard, bassists Reggie Workman and Art Davis, and the great Eric Dolphy on flute and alto sax. It was the title track that caught my ear. Extending over the whole side A of the album, it’s a modal feast that builds on a vamp derived from a Spanish folk song. Here, it starts with a single churning bass line and Tyner’s pulsating chords balancing on Jones' driving swing. Soon, Coltrane joins on soprano sax with an approach reminiscent of his playing on ‘My Favorite Things.’ Then, Dolphy lends his flute to the mix, paving the way for Hubbard’s solo, from which the track really takes off. It was rhythmically dense music, but not overly dissonant or harsh; however, for ears that could listen to jazz but were more attuned to rock, it was the perfect hook - a little more advanced than what I was used to, but not too steep of a climb. The B-side’s, ‘Dahomey Dance’ and ‘Aisha’ were a bit more rooted in the ‘jazz’ I knew. I enjoyed them, but it was the A-side that pushed me as a listener. Critics have called Olé a transitional album. Aside from the label change, Coltrane was also headed towards more experimental realms. For me, Olé and that pile of records also came at a transitional time, and helped reveal new paths and possibilities. Thelonious Monk with John Coltrane (Jazzland, 1961) My plan was to next dig into something in that experimental realm. I had my sights on Offering: Live at Temple University, a live album recorded in 1966, shortly before Coltrane passed away, and released posthumously by Resonance Records in 2014. A funny thing happened, however, along the way. As I was pulling up the recording, I passed by Thelonious Monk with John Coltrane and stopped in my tracks. Also released in 1961 on the Jazzland label, this set of evergreen Monk tunes that had been recorded by Coltrane and Monk in '57 and '58 with changing rhythm sections. Two seconds of the opening ‘Ruby, My Dear’ and I knew I’d wanted to spend a little time awith this one again before moving on. As the story goes, Coltrane was addicted to heroin and had just been fired from Miles Davis’ group. He took this break, and cleaned himself up and started to play with Monk. A residency at the Five Spot in NYC in ‘57 is the stuff of legends and a concert recording of the two from 1957 was discovered and released in 2005 by Blue Note, lends credence to the stories. Entitled Thelonious Monk Quartet with John Coltrane at Carnegie Hall, it underscores the copacetic musical relationship found on the original release. Back to that recording: the tune that stopped me in my tracks, the slow moving ‘Ruby, My Dear’ begins with such a melancholic saxophone playing the yearning melody that it instantly romanticizes any space where it’s played. ‘Tinkle, Tinkle,’ with its playful and up-tempo melody gives Coltrane a chance to unfurl those ‘sheets of sound’ that he’s famous for. Similarly on ‘Nutty’, the sheets return in a generously flowing solo, studded at key points with with reminders of the melody. Drum and bass outlining the tune, Monk waiting to come back in with the melody, before abstracting it into Improvisational flurries. This album album is a high point in two musical catalogs that are festooned with them. Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以西班牙民歌为素材展开长达整面的模态即兴演奏，低音线条持续推进，钢琴和弦悬于鼓点之上。科尔曼以高音萨克斯开场，演奏方式令人联想到《My Favorite Things》中的处理，随后多尔菲的长笛与哈伯德的小号独奏将作品推向高潮。整体节奏密集但不刺耳，在不和谐与可听性之间找到平衡点，既具备爵士深度又不失对摇滚听众的亲和力。评论者认为这是科尔曼转型期的作品——既是他转向更实验领域的过渡，也是一段个人音乐启蒙的记录。B面两首作品更贴近传统爵士语汇，但A面始终是推动听众成长的核心力量。整篇文章以个人回忆为线索，将这张唱片置于生命转变的节点上，探讨了它如何打开了新的聆听维度与人生可能。

items.body: Footfalls (Miasmah, November 22) is a collaboration between Gareth Davis and Scanner. The pair present two scenes, loosely inspired by the poets and novelists T.S Elliot and Samuel Beckett and taken from differing sides of the same desolate seaside setting. In the grip of winter, the seaside slants, becoming bleak, and it’s a sharp contrast from an endless summer, with lifeless, empty harbours and thick clumps of seaweed hanging from the crests of cold waves. The water temperature has dropped to that of ice in liquid form. This desolation manifests through a bass clarinet – played by Gareth Davis – and its long, slinking drone stretches the music, causing it to echo through a rainy day and along soggy sand. Tourists don’t see this side of the beach, and the music reflects this. As ever, Scanner (Robin Rimbaud) provides an impressive range of electronic oscillations and manipulations. Sound waves ride shotgun on their own tides, pulsing and then falling back, bubbling up and receding into nothingness, sometimes bringing the staccato of dashes and dots, and other times shrouding the clarinet’s tone in an electronic-made fog that comes rolling off the ocean, pulsing, glowing. John Carpenter would be proud. The sharp synths that enter seven or so minutes into the eighteen-minute opener ‘Towards The Door’ cut through the electronics, coming out of nowhere and rising up over the cold beach. The wail of a siren. The change in register lifts the music up, even if it’s just a temporary perch, and there’s no forewarning to it, which increases the sense of unease. For the most part, it remains low, stuck in the gloom of an overcast day, dank and grey. This won’t appear on the postcards when summer season rolls around. Towards the end, the artificial sounds of the sea bleed out, and the authentic sound of the sea’s waves replace the electronic waves via field recordings of the ocean. Although the lapping of the shore is calming and ambient (Eno didn’t create ambient music – nature did), frequently used in meditation and rest, it feels a little cooler here, a little disquieting. The whole piece is mesmerising. ‘Smokefall’ is more voice-oriented, as it repeats and distorts a running phrase. Like some kind of nightmarish mantra, the voice lies in the background, barely audible, a radio signal or a police band picked up by an amplifier and hijacked by accident. The electronics are more jagged here, providing a scratchy rhythm of their own: we’ve gone past the seafront and now stand beside the cliffs, walking around the top of the promenade for a better view…although it’s still largely the same, a grey, rolling mass covering the entire horizon. Environments affect the mind and its emotional tides, positively, negatively, or nonchalantly, and this bank of water does little to lift the tonal depression. Although the bass clarinet has more of a range and chooses to move around a bit more, it’s still not overly flexible, and the electronics wrap it up, constricting it. In fact, Scanner’s electronics are central to this piece. Although prolific, these two musicians never seem to run out of ideas. Footfalls is another step in the right direction. www.miasmah.com
items._cn_summary: 《Footfalls》是低音单簧管演奏家Gareth Davis与电子音乐人Scanner合作的专辑，灵感源自T.S.艾略特与贝克特的文学意象。Davis的低音单簧管发出绵长蜿蜒的嗡鸣，在阴冷潮湿的海滨荒凉感中延展开来；Scanner则提供了从振荡脉冲到颗粒噪声的多层次电子声响处理。两首作品分别以器乐延伸与语言失真为线索，前者在十八分钟里逐步引入合成器尖啸与真实的海浪田野录音作为电子音景的自然过渡，后者通过人声循环与电子刮擦构建夜魇般的氛围。整体氛围沉郁、克制，呈现出冬季海岸的灰冷色调，将器乐即兴、磁场磁带美学与环境录音融为一体。

items.body: Acclimation, or acclimatisation as it is more commonly termed, is a process by which an individual organism adjusts to a change in its environment. This could be the response of an animal or plant to a change of season; the adaptation of a mountaineer to a high-altitude atmosphere; or, perhaps more obliquely, the ‘becoming natural’ of certain introduced objects or processes (consider how, for many observers of the British landscape, treeless fields and dry stone walls have ‘acclimated’ to their environment and thus become ‘natural’, while wind turbines have yet to do so). The latter example may be somewhat spurious, but it is relevant to the themes and processes behind Jake Muir’s new album. The Seattle-based artist was inspired by the invitation to perform at the century-old Georgetown Steam Plant to create a live set based on industrial and aqueous field recordings, and this set became the basis of “Acclimation”. Without knowing this context, however, it would be difficult to link the album’s two tracks back to any kind of industrial activity; on the contrary, Muir has arranged and processed his sounds such that they come to resemble a more general enveloping environment. Mechanical, electronic, and ecological effects overrun their respective boundaries and blur the perceptual and conceptual lines between them. What does this sound like in practice? ‘Cold Seeps’ presents a dense, humid tropical atmosphere, with damp gleaming and splish-splashes of water, the brushing of leaves and snapping of twigs. None of these things are heard, exactly; rather, a rich field of abstract sound suggests or gestures towards such things. Later on in the piece, a faint ringing glimmer builds into an emphatic high-pitched stutter, and gleaming winds race over low bass throb, evoking more a weather system on another planet, or a moon such as Titan or Enceladus, than anywhere on Earth. Towards the end, however, bright, undulating tones recall sharp sunlight and the rolling of the sea, a postcard from the Pacific coast reduced to smudged outlines and splotches of colour. A similar approach to rhythm informs ‘Black Smokers’, the vague tossing and turning of which has more in common with outdoor environments than the strictly regulated pulse of most Western music. A faint crackle recalls quiet, hesitant footsteps on gravel or sand, and tones soar like the cries of distant birds. Things rattle and echo as if on the floor of a vast canyon, or tap intermittently like a moored boat’s rigging against a mast. Harmony is sometimes present, though somewhat effaced, or rather transformed: glistening tones gather in what sometimes resemble chords, but also gusts, flocks, streams. Perhaps it’s just my own idiosyncratic way of listening to it, but to me it seems that with “Acclimation” Muir has succeeded in bringing the ‘industrial’ and the ‘natural’ together in ways that sound like neither, but somehow lean decidedly towards the latter; I’d be interested in hearing what impressions it forms on other listening ears. Acclimation by Jake Muir Jake Muir Dragon’s Eye Recordings
items._genre: ambient / field recording / experimental electronic / industrial
items._cn_summary: Jake Muir受邀在西雅图百年历史的Georgetown蒸汽厂演出，以此为灵感创作了《Acclimation》专辑。整张专辑仅有两首曲目，基于工业与水声田野录音进行深度处理与重组。艺术家并未让原始声音直接指向工业场景，而是将机械、电子与生态声响相互渗透融合，营造出一种模糊边界的包覆式环境感。《Cold Seeps》构建出潮湿的热带氛围，水滴、枝叶声响以抽象音场的方式被暗示；中段高频颤音与低频脉动交织，联想到外星天气的奇异景象。《Black Smokers》则以非规则节奏模拟户外环境，风声、碎石脚步、鸟鸣、船桅碰撞等意象在抽象音色中若隐若现。整张专辑模糊了工业与自然的感知界限，是一次关于声响转化的细致实验。

items.body: Palagoma is not only the first release from Nairobi-based label Cool Waters, it also marks the first time German-born, Kenya-based percussionist Sven Kacirek has collaborated with Ogoya Nengo and Olith Ratengo at the same time. Odd Okoddo, the duo of Kacirek and Ratengo, has been performing since 2018, but with the inclusion of the 83 year old Nengo, a singer from the eastern part of the country, there�s an added traditional depth to the music. A 2025 performance shows Nengo�s lifetime of experience singing Kenya�s dodo tradition around 2 and half minutes in (see below). Furthermore, her inclusion on this album allows her and Ratengo to toss the vocals back and forth as they reference their shared roots (Ratengo and Nengo live minutes from each other). Musically, however, the tracks are driven by Kacirek�s Buchla synth, hand percussion, and occasional kit drumming, which serve to buoy the voices without blotting out the music�s origins. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Bara,� for example, begins with the dime-store thwack of a repeated pattern, a stiff juxtaposition to the voices; yet, as the song rolls along, a 4/4 clink appears, then a burbling bass, and finally, what sounds like a xylophone. Layers of synthesized polyrhythms keep presenting themselves with a subtlety almost unnoticeable, until, by the track�s end, it feels organic, as if it�s all been underneath the two voices all along. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Sarah,� perhaps the album�s most intense track, features a lead vocal from Ratengo and tentative, percussive spittles from Kacirek. And while the technology never tries to overtake the vocals, it does sneak up and punctuate the track�s urgency, as edgy distortion sneaks in here and there just as Ratengo�s voice reaches its peak. The term �folktronica� has been bandied about as a way to house the type of music on offer here. In fact, exploratory collaborations such as Chouk Bwa & The �ngstr�mers as well as much of Kampala, Uganda�s Nyege Nyege label house sounds that might be �folktronic� in some way. What�s more interesting and important about this music, though, is how truly global so much of it is while maintaining a deep connection to Africa and its diasporic communities. The music on Palagoma , as well as much of what�s linked above (and available in countless other recent recordings) demonstrates a real willingness for cultures to respond to each other without trampling traditions altogether. Instead, roots become avant-garde and innovations become seemingly thousands of years old. Certainly the inclusion of an 83 year old traditional Kenyan singer only recently making her global debut as she tours with a duo whose instrumental voice is a white male saturated in electronic Kenyan rhythms demonstrates this blurring. The music this trio makes is certainly of the 21st century, but it�s often hazy, sparse, and open, keeping it from a quick sell-by date or confining it to a specific genre. Instead, it�s a beautiful example music as grace.
items.label: Cool Waters
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是内罗毕厂牌Cool Waters的首发作品，由德国出生、肯尼亚定居的打击乐手Sven Kacirek与奥利特·拉滕戈组成二人组Odd Okoddo，并邀请83岁东部肯尼亚传统多朵歌唱传承人奥戈亚·嫩戈共同录制。三人以人声对话为核心，卡齐雷克使用Buchla合成器、手打打击乐与偶尔的架子鼓构建层层递进的合成复合节奏，既托举人声又不淹没根源。专辑中歌曲从简约节奏型起，逐步叠加4/4敲击、低音线、木琴质感的音色层，最终形成有机统一的整体。乐评将这种创作方式与Chouk Bwa及Nyege Nyege厂牌的探索性合作并置，指出其核心价值在于跨文化对话中既保持与非洲传统的深度联结，又实现前卫化的声音探索，使根源本身呈现出未来感与千年古老感并存的双重面貌。

items.album: Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari
items.artist: Dorothy Moskowitz & United States of Alchemy
items.excerpt:
Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release,
Under an Endless Sky
.
In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari,
Songs of Compassion
is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics.
Francesco Paolo Paladi
items.body: Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release, Under an Endless Sky . In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari, Songs of Compassion is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics. Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari | Photo by Maria Assunta Karini Songs of Compassion has two challenges for the listener. The first is the music, called variously avant-garde, ambient, modal, non-linear, and a few more. It is played mostly on pianos mixed in and out of the foreground, sometimes doubled, and sometimes out of phase, joined by strings, woodwinds, synth washes, and steely sounds. Initially disorienting, the music serves to remind us how locked our minds are to Western notions of harmonic movement. It speaks of alternative musical narratives much older and much further away. They are songs that subvert the song: more like Steve Reich than Steve Stills; more like Phillip Glass than Phil Collins. UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY - Pale Wanderer At the same time, there are the poetic yet strikingly contemporary lyrics. �Pale Wanderer� talks about the fact that authoritarianism needs willing accomplices, describing what happens �When you make a deal with darkness.� UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY (Dorothy Moskowitz, Francesco Paolo Paladino e Luka Chino Ferrari) by Silentes �Charlottesville� (written with the late Joe Byrd) evokes the time not long ago when torch-wielding nazis, proud of the metaphoric Ns on their tunics, chanted the antisemitic tropes paraphrased in Moskowitz�s words, �We�ll be one people, pure of race/No greedy throng could take our place� . Besides the overtly political lyrics, in the tradition of 1960s protest songs, there are also thoughtful meditations on mortality and our place in the universe. The message is high-minded yet sincere and direct. World weary and wise, Moskowitz�s voice inhabits the evocative philosophical lyrics with the authority of a skilled method actor. The melodies unfold like streams of consciousness, rising and falling, not following expected diatonic chord progressions, but honouring, instead, the value of each word. Moskowitz�s piano acts as another voice and sometimes a kind of Greek chorus commenting on the proceedings. The surrounding music frames, creates pulses and dissonances, and shimmers. The return of Dorothy Moskowitz with her renamed project has arrived in a moment quite similar to the times that spawned its predecessor. Political division, unrest, and uncertainty always generate artistic reaction, and United States of Alchemy roared back to life with their epic 24-minute opening track �Under an Endless Sky� in 2023, serving perhaps as an �In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida� for our times. Songs of Compassion continues to challenge how we think about our world. It�s music that defies the song form, while doing exactly what music is supposed to do�enrich the human condition. Find the artist online. The title track from the 2023 U.S. of Alchemy recording Under an Endless Sky by Dorothy Moskowitz & United States of Alchemy Further reading Cris Derksen - The Visit (Review) Tiny Sun - Vanishment (Review) Maria Ka - Di Mashin (Review) Further listening You will find a number of Dorothy Moskowitz's works on Race The Sky , most recently on Podgrammes #022 and #019.
items.label: Songs of Compassion
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是Dorothy Moskowitz与意大利前卫作曲家Francesco Paolo Paladino及诗人Luca Chino Ferrari的合作项目，包含十一首歌曲。音乐以钢琴为核心，辅以弦乐、木管、合成器铺陈和金属质感音色，采用非线性的调式手法，打破西方和声进行的惯性思维，呈现出介于Steve Reich与Philip Glass之间的简约重复美学。人声演唱如意识流般起伏，不遵循常规的音阶进行，而是服务于每个词语的内在含义。歌词兼具政治性与哲思，既直指当代权威主义的合谋机制与白人至上主义的暴力，也探讨死亡与人在宇宙中的位置。Moskowitz的钢琴演奏如同另一重声部，扮演希腊悲剧中歌队的角色，对叙事进行评注。整体而言，这是一张融合诗歌、前卫作曲与时事关怀的作品，植根于1960年代抗议音乐传统，又以现代声音美学重新诠释。

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — One of the most unique and stranger acts to emerge from the 70s prog scene was bizarre in many waysactually. AKASHA emerged from Norway, a nation currently prolific to progressive music in the 21stcentury wasn't a major player in the golden years of prog rock. And this band didn't come from Oslo,This short-lived act came from one of the most northern regions of all of Europe and formed in thesmall Arctic fishing village of Kj�llefjord. But what makes this band strange is that it reallydidn't sound like any other act of the day despite smatterings of influences piled into the schizoidrandom musical styles that seemed to find bits and pieces derived from Genesis, Pink Floyd, TheMoody Blues and King Crimson amongst others. The band was a quintet featuring Sverre Svendsen onlead vocals and mellotrons, Jens Ivar Andreassen on guitars, Mellotron, synthesizers, piano, organ,Arild Andreassen on bass, Kjell Evensen on drums and also included are the lyrics and poetry of Tor-Jony Hansen. AKASHA released only one mere album in 1977 and given its extreme remote location with littleopportunity for promotion or touring for that matter, the album has become one of those extremerarities. The strange artifact is also unique in that it displays the track listings on the frontcover but what really sets this one apart is the mishmash of music sounds that include hypnoticspace rock, freaky sound generated through synthesizers and mellotrons and a schizophrenic hairpinpropensity to simply morph into other music styles midstream reminding me a bit of the GermanKrautrock act Silberbart albeit with less guitar bombast. Likewise the band recorded in a bomb-proofcellar which was used as a shelter in the basement of a hotel in the small town of Finnsnes, Norwaywhich gives the production an interesting uniqueness much in the way of the band German Oak whichrecorded in a similar bomb shelter.The lengthy "Isle Of Kawi" begins the epic journey sounding something like the French Archaĩa withrapid fire synthesized arpeggios and what sounds like some sort of folk music but then sort ofshifts gears and sounds a bit more like something Pulsar would've conjured up on the first tworeleases. With this opening track it feels like you've stumbled into some lost classic musical treatas the sonic display is brooding and dark and on par with early Univers Zero for apocalyptic motifsof complete detachment from established paradigms. The track continues to morph into a labyrinthinedisplay of interesting twists and turns. The album quickly reveals its greatest flaw though on thesecond track "Bondage" which finds the lackluster vocal style of Sverre Svendsen who delivers arather mopey scatter-brained performance over some sort of drugged out lounge music before the trackbursts into rapid-fire key arpeggios that prognosticate the work of Philip Glass on "Glassworks" andhis classic "Koyaanisqatsi." And then off to some early "Trespass" styled Genesis sounding prog!The instrumental combo effect of "Recitativ" and "Electronic Nightmare" displays the band at itsmost unhinged with the first track in full rock mode for the first time only with strange guitarriffs and off-kilter contrapuntal elements. Unlike the prior tracks, this one has pounding drums anda guitar solo. The second on the other hand goes into outer space and features avant-gardeexperimentalism carried out through overlayering electronic effects sounding more Tangerine Dream orKlaus Schulze with a steady rhythmic pulse of Jean Michel Jarre. "Death Hymn" combines faster rockwith the electronics and then breaks into some sort of rockin' the classics keyboard freneticismmore in vein of The Nice. But wait! There's more - it then morphs into a slow oozing space rockmotif with detached spoken word lyrics which are in English. "Light And Darkness" is one of the mostschizoid tracks with several changes of tempos, styles and rich in off-kilter time signatures andjust plain bonkers ideas. More steeped in rock but drenched in mellotrons and atmospheric weirdnessas well."The Trip" offers the most normal track on board and actually sticks to a bluesy rock format formost of its run however the closing "Man And The Void" however returns to the restless nature of thealbum with a space rock intro that quickly shifts into strange guitar chord riffs and at timesreminds me of Gnidrolog but less structured and more freeform in many ways. This album offers thetrue spirit of DIY musical ambitions overcoming the extreme remote geography, lack of recordingfacilities and production extravaganzas. This band truly did things its own way on its own terms.Despite the imperfections of weak vocals, lackluster production and blatant disregard for any sortof unified sound, this album will appeal to those seeking out the most unapologetically originalalbums of the era and despite the flaws more than makes up for in its sheer creative audacity thatmakes AKASHA really a difficult band to classify with its symphonic prog, Krautrock and eclecticmusic spirit. For my tastes this one is quite appealing.
items._genre: psychedelic rock / space rock / progressive rock / krautrock
items._cn_summary: AKASHA 1977年唯一专辑出自挪威北极圈小渔村Kjøllefjord，录制于当地旅馆的防空掩体地下室，造就了独特的声学质感。乐队五人配置融合大量合成器、mellotron与键盘，主唱风格懒散迷离，音乐在迷幻太空摇滚、Krautrock自由即兴与前卫摇滚之间不断跳转变形。开场曲'Isle Of Kawi'以快速合成器琶音开场，氛围阴郁而宏大，接近法国前卫乐队Archaïa与Univers Zero的世界末日感；中段风格突变，类比Philip Glass的极简重复音型与Genesis早期作品的交织。乐队坦承的影响来源包括Genesis、Pink Floyd、Moody Blues与King Crimson，但实际呈现却与任何同期乐队都明显不同。因地理位置极端偏远，缺乏宣传与巡演机会，专辑已成为极度稀有的藏品。整体听感如同迷失在时间裂缝中偶然发现的听觉遗物，结构松散却充满意外的转折。

items.body: Mexico City producer Dimitri Berzerk released his second full-length album, “Así en la Tierra como en el Cielo” (“As on Earth, So in Heaven”), on September 24, 2026, through his own label, Sector Industrial Producciones (SIP). The eleven-track record blends synthpop and industrial elements in a style Berzerk calls “Esoteric Body Music.” He built the release as a concept album accompanied by a printed book, with illustrations by Amanda Lunares. The label’s own description characterizes the album as music “seeking to illuminate the dark paths within us and help us rediscover what has been lost.” Berzerk describes Esoteric Body Music as the balance point between synthpop and industrial, tied to concepts drawn from philosophy, alchemy, astrology, and sacred geometry. Tracklist and credits for ‘Así en la Tierra como en el Cielo’ The album has eleven tracks: “Inevitabilis,” “Surgere,” “Statera,” “Solvere,” “Syzygia,” “Intemerata,” “Coniunctio,” “Coagulatio,” “Concordia,” “Cadere,” and “Insanabilis.” Berzerk wrote, composed and recorded the songs in Mexico City between 2024 and 2025, except “Cadere,” co-written with Mexican musician Hari Sama in 2024. Traditional Hindu texts appear on “Inevitabilis.” Fragments on “Surgere,” “Statera,” “Intemerata,” “Concordia” and “Cadere” come from “The Book of Tokens” by Paul Foster Case. Sergio García and Quetzalcoatl Gutiérrez mixed and mastered the album in Dolby Atmos at Studio Quetzalcoatl in Mexico City. Berzerk designed the album concept and the accompanying book himself; Amanda Lunares created the artwork and illustrations. Guest vocalists include Pedro Dabdoub on “Inevitabilis,” Pedro Gopar of Prismatic Shapes on “Surgere,” Pascal Languirand of Trans-X on “Statera,” Amanda Lunares on “Solvere,” Heka on “Syzygia,” Montse Magia on “Intemerata,” and Norms Dom on “Coniunctio.” Additional musicians include Chuz Estrada on drums (“Inevitabilis,” “Statera”), Guillermo Torres on guitar (“Surgere”), Raul García on guitar (“Cadere”), Helena Sánchez Soto on vocal arrangements (“Insanabilis”), and Adrián Díaz Hilton on choir arrangements (“Insanabilis”). Gustavo Cid recorded voice on “Coniunctio”; Moises Navarro recorded voice on “Intemerata” and “Insanabilis.” A concept album with an accompanying book “Así en la Tierra como en el Cielo” is built as a concept album. The book that accompanies it uses Amanda Lunares’ illustrations as symbols tied to the album’s themes. SIP states the album explores emotion and perception together, continuing the philosophical and esoteric direction of Berzerk’s earlier work. Physical CD-and-book edition planned SIP states a physical edition is coming, in a CD-and-book package, following the same approach used on Berzerk’s previous album. His 2023 debut full-length, “Nineteen Eighty-Four,” was also released in book format, according to the Mexican outlet Casete.com.mx. No release date, order link, or pricing for the physical edition of “Así en la Tierra como en el Cielo” has been confirmed. Where to hear ‘Así en la Tierra como en el Cielo’ The album streams and is available to download on Bandcamp. SIP’s promotional material describes the album as available “across all music platforms,” but as of publication the album could not be found on Spotify or Apple Music, where several of Berzerk’s earlier releases, including “Nineteen Eighty-Four” and “The Liquid Path,” are listed. Wider platform availability for the new album is unconfirmed. About Dimitri Berzerk Dimitri Berzerk is the recording name of Dimitri Loyo, a DJ, producer, remixer and label owner based in Mexico City. He told Side-Line in a 2021 interview that the name “Berzerk” draws on the Atari video game of the same name, his first exposure to vocoders, and on the Norwegian band Apoptygma Berzerk, an act he likes. The two are unrelated projects. Berzerk began DJing in 2005, performing at nightclubs, festivals and on radio across Mexico, with more than a thousand performances across the Americas and northern Europe, according to Casete.com.mx. From 2009 he produced remixes under the alias DMT Berzerk, releasing more than a hundred of them, including eight remix compilation volumes issued on physical formats through Conzoom Records (Germany) and Subterrane Records (Australia), both now out of print. Under his own name, Berzerk founded Sector Industrial Producciones and released three EPs on the label by mid-2021. SIP also issued “Remixes Collection Vol.02” (May 2018) and “Remixes Collection Vol.03” on CD (October 2018), both reviewed on Side-Line. From 2019 he began releasing original material under the Dimitri Berzerk name, with eight singles and EPs issued on CD, vinyl and digital through Norwegian label Sub Culture Records. In November 2022, he became a third member of Mexican act C-Lekktor, alongside Markko and Jamie. Berzerk released his debut full-length album, “Nineteen Eighty-Four,” on March 3, 2023, compiling and reworking tracks from his earlier EPs with guest vocalists including Claus Larsen. Side-Line’s review called it a blend of “danceable electro-pop with harder EBM songs” and rated it 8/10. Casete.com.mx reported the album was also presented in book format. Berzerk followed it with the “Resist” EP in October 2024, released via SIP in digital, CD and vinyl formats, again featuring Claus Larsen on guest vocals. “Así en la Tierra como en el Cielo,” released September 24, 2026, is Berzerk’s second full-length album and continues the concept-album-and-book format he used on “Nineteen Eighty-Four.”

items.body: Distort Everything Forever opens in ambience, spends most of its middle throwing rhythmic and low frequency chaos at you, then returns toward atmosphere at the end. The record opens a door, destroys the room, then leaves you in the wreckage Distort Everything Forever by SUAHN   SUAHN is Michael York, Baltimore-based, and his music has been moving through bass music, acid, techno, jungle, and experimental club forms long enough that Distort Everything Forever doesn’t arrive sounding like a debut. York grew up hearing hand-me-down mix CDs from his uncle, Aphex Twin and Venetian Snares sitting next to The Cure and Bauhaus on the same tape. That detail explains a lot about the harsher edges of what he makes. Four Tet, RL Grime, Ivy Lab, and Boombox Cartel have all picked up his catalog. He appeared on VISION‘s MISSION 03 compilation alongside Billain, Posij, Current Value, and others. So the full-length context is already there before a single track plays. The opener “Reverie” starts in ambience. Gives the impression things might unfold slowly. That doesn’t last. Heavy bass, drum and bass breaks, distorted percussion, hip hop rhythmic ideas, it arrives fast and stays physical for most of the runtime. York doesn’t spend time introducing himself. The drums show up and the record commits. The title is a literal description of the production language. Distortion isn’t decoration here, it bleeds into everything. Drums, bass, breaks, vocal fragments, transitional material. At a certain point it stops being an effect and becomes the identity of the record. There’s drum and bass underneath a lot of this, but also half-time hip hop programming, bass music, and the heavier side of experimental club production. Points where it touches the same territory as VISION releases—beat-driven material where drum and bass structure gets slowed, stretched apart, and rebuilt around enormous low end. “Drifting” is where the album properly declares itself. Old school drum and bass instinct in the way it moves. Not especially melodic, doesn’t need to be. The drums do most of the talking. Filter sweeps and frequency movement pull you further in gradually, and York trusts the breaks to establish the personality of the track without constantly dropping another melodic idea on top. That restraint is what makes the track land. “Lost in it All” goes heavier. Half-time rhythms, bass with real dub-like weight, distortion threatening to tear it apart at the edges. This is where the VISION comparison becomes most useful, the heavier beat-focused side of NOISIA‘s label, where sound design carries as much importance as composition and a bass hit functions almost like a lead instrument. York understands that language. The saturation and distortion give his version a dirtier edge than most producers working in that space would allow. The tracks sound filthy because they’re supposed to :: Worth noting what heavy distortion actually costs at the mix stage. Once you start saturating bass, drums, and midrange simultaneously, everything generates additional harmonics that compete for the same frequency space. Transients lose definition. Low mids turn to mud. The challenge is making something sound destroyed while still giving every important element enough room to be understood. York handles this well, the tracks sound filthy because they’re supposed to, but the kicks still hit, the bass still has shape, and the breaks never collapse into an undefined wall of noise. That kind of control doesn’t happen accidentally. “How Dark it Gets” is another standout, specifically for the vocal work. Fragments getting chopped, repositioned, distorted, thrown against the breaks, the edits never become a gimmick because they function as another rhythmic layer. Small pieces surface, disappear, return processed differently. The track feels like it’s constantly rearranging itself while you’re inside it. What becomes clear across the full runtime is how studied York is in this corner of electronic music. The Aphex Twin and Venetian Snares references from his background make sense, but this isn’t an IDM record in the older Warp or Rephlex sense. The center of gravity is heavier, connected to modern bass production, jungle, drum and bass, industrial club music, and the post-NOISIA school of extremely controlled sound design. Someone who understands what happens when breaks become texture, when distortion becomes arrangement, when bass stops functioning as low end and starts carrying the emotional weight of a track. The sequencing does real work too. Distort Everything Forever opens in ambience, spends most of its middle throwing rhythmic and low frequency chaos at you, then returns toward atmosphere at the end. The quiet at the beginning and the quiet at the end aren’t the same quiet. Everything that happened between them changes what the stillness means. The record opens a door, destroys the room, then leaves you in the wreckage. That’s a complete thought. Distort Everything Forever is available on Bandcamp. Distort Everything Forever by SUAHNThe post SUAHN :: Distort Everything Forever (Self Released) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items._cn_summary: SUAHN（巴尔的摩制作人Michael York）的全长专辑以环境氛围开场，迅速切入低频混乱与碎拍节奏的密集轰炸，尾声回归氛围层次。失真不是装饰而是核心语言，渗透进鼓、贝斯、人声碎片和过渡素材中，使效果本身成为作品身份。专辑涵盖鼓打贝斯、半拍嘻哈编程、重型bass music与实验俱乐部制作，靠近VISION厂牌（NOISIA旗下）的厚重节拍取向。《Drifting》展示oldschool鼓打贝斯的克制与断片张力，《Lost in it All》则走向更重的dub感低频与饱和失真边缘。York以粗粝的声音设计区别于同领域多数制作人，在结构与打击感的对话中保持强劲身体性。

items.body: Review by arcane-beautiful — Terrifying Angels by Pure Reason Revolution sees the band making their darkest and heaviest album to date, but still keeping specific musical quirks that the band are known for. Taking their new prog sound into elements that include dark ambient, nu metal, psychedelic, symphonic and alternative rock, it proves that Jon Courtney's project still has heavy weight and impression. The trade off of vocals between Courtney & Annicke Shireen are mixed perfectly, with great depth and tone, while musically the band explore all aspects of their sound, making this a true stand out in their discography. While the longer tracks are the true attention grabbers, the shorter songs do keep to their more classic sound with heavier elements. I'd give this a low to mid 8 out of 10. The track I'd recommend is Terrifying Angels.
items._genre: crossover prog / dark ambient / nu metal / psychedelic / alternative rock
items._cn_summary: Pure Reason Revolution的这张专辑被描述为乐队迄今最黑暗、最沉重的作品，同时保留了其标志性的音乐特质。专辑将前卫摇滚的根基拓展至暗氛围、新金属、迷幻、交响及另类摇滚等多个领域，显示出项目主脑Jon Courtney在声音探索上的深度与分量。人声层面由Courtney与Annicke Shireen交替承担，两者在音色与情感深度上实现了良好的平衡。专辑结构上，较长的曲目承担了主要的听觉张力，较短的作品则回归乐队经典框架并融入更重的元素，形成长短交错的编排策略。整体而言，这是一张在乐队既有体系内进行多向延伸的作品，强调重量感与氛围感的双重塑造。

items.body: It has been about four years since the Brazilian act Aesthetische released their last full-length album, but in the meantime, Gui Pires and Fab Viscardi have kept us entertained with an annual EP. “Every Beat Matters” serves as a metaphor for everything we can do to fight injustice, fascism, prejudice, war, and more. Musically, this translates into four brand-new tracks followed by three remixes. Aesthetische return to their roots more than ever, recalling their former project, Aghast View, with a sound deeply rooted in EBM. It is a meticulously crafted production boasting rich soundscapes and razor-sharp basslines that once again bring Front Line Assembly to mind. The tracks are driven by stomping beats that give them maximum club appeal. To my ears, the first three tracks all sound like potential singles, although Aesthetische clearly have a soft spot for “Chew The Loop,” which appears in three additional and strong remixes. The vocals round everything out, complemented by well-placed samples. One track remains instrumental, yet sounds incredibly effective. Aesthetische never disappoint, but this new EP is undoubtedly one of their strongest releases to date. It represents intelligent, impactful EBM. (Rating:9). Side-Line reported the release of “Every Beat Matters” on June 26, 2026 via Alfa Matrix. Listen to “Chew The Loop”’: Chew The Loop by Aesthetische About Aesthetische Aesthetische is a Brazilian EBM/industrial duo formed by Gui Pires and Fab Viscardi in 2012. Both musicians were previously known for their work in Aghast View and Biopsy, one of Brazil’s pioneering electro-industrial acts of the 1990s. After Aghast View, the duo launched Aesthetische as a new vehicle for modern EBM fused with trance, techno-body music, and industrial atmospheres. The band signed with Belgian label Alfa Matrix in 2012 and has since maintained an exclusive release partnership with them, issuing a steady discography of albums, EPs, and digital singles across physical and digital formats. Albums “Powerswitch” (2012, Alfa Matrix) – Issued in multiple editions, including a box version. “HybridCore” (2014, Alfa Matrix) – A follow-up blending hard-hitting EBM with more melodic synth textures. “Co3xist3ns3” (2019, Alfa Matrix) – Marked a return after several years, further exploring hybridized EBM and trance. “Rvprty” (2022, Alfa Matrix AM 3400DJ) – A digital-only release containing ten tracks. Singles & EPs “Nachtbrenner” (2013, Alfa Matrix) “Statement / Amplitude Zero” (2013, Alfa Matrix) “Colder Lights EP” (2014, Alfa Matrix) “Dirt And Basslines” (2015, Alfa Matrix) “Cold Is Clean” (2015, Alfa Matrix) “We Follow Blindly” (2016, Alfa Matrix) “In My Aurora” (2017, Alfa Matrix) – Featuring Noemi Aurora on vocals. “MMXX” (2020, Alfa Matrix) “Overflow” (2021, Alfa Matrix) “Boiling Over EP” (2023, Alfa Matrix) “Confidence Is Silent” (2024, Alfa Matrix) Split EP “4.4U [2012.11]” (2012, Alfa Matrix) – Digital compilation shared with Metroland, Mentallo & The Fixer, and Daniel B. Prothèse. Alfa Matrix has continued the pace since, following “Boiling Over” (2023) with “Confidence Is Silent” (2024), “Selling Fear” (2025) and now “Every Beat Matters” in 2026.
items._cn_summary: 巴西双人组Aesthetische时隔四年再度发行EP，以四首新作加三首混音的构架延续其EBM根基。制作上回归早期Aghast View时期的硬朗路线，低频线条锋利，节奏紧凑，强调俱乐部场景的能量。题材层面将反对不公、法西斯与战争的态度嵌入节拍之中，以音乐行动作为隐喻。首三首曲目具备单曲潜质，标题曲《Chew The Loop》被多次混音再诠释，显示厂牌对单曲传播力的重视。人声与采样层叠有序，器乐曲目亦维持推进力。整体定位为智能化、冲击力强的EBM作品，是乐队阵容中较具说服力的一次短篇呈现。

items.body: Deep utterances and smoky melodies fill the old courtyards of Jozef Van Wissem’s music. On Nobody Living Can Ever Make Me Turn Back (Consouling Sounds), the lute’s spidery melodies appear as finely woven webs, echoing into the present from the distant past. Something is brewing. An explosive beat rocks the medieval sound to its core, less a queasy shake and more like a 7.o earthquake. The misty and quietly revolutionary tones carry the ill weight of death. The melodies themselves are almost like the Black Death, spreading throughout the eastern European townships of the album and going door-to-door, knocking lightly like a strange, dark-coated preacher – ‘you will come with me now’, it says – as the sickening fog leaves behind nothing but stark, quiet streets and stained doors, a field of hastily-painted crosses traced along both sides. Clammy-faced inhabitants are locked inside otherwise empty rooms, and a row of filled tombs line the music, track by track. There is something incredibly earthy to the sound, like century-old soil. Nobody Living Can Ever Make Me Turn Back takes its inspiration from a painting by Belgian artist Cindy Wright (her painting is the one on the cover). Things are delicate here, as delicate and as temporary as a note on a quivering string before it fades into permanent silence, into its flame-streaked sunset, ultimately moving into the death of itself and its subsequent absorption into the earth and air. Nothing lasts forever, and the skull on the cover testifies to that. Van Wissem’s music plucks a very distinct chord. The notes are splayed out like an ancient victim on a medieval rack, but there’s more of an emphasis on pleasure rather than on pain, with echoing vocals calling out from a cold, lantern-lit chamber, soaking into the cold slabs of stone, and the masterful playing of the lute ringing through the draughty corridors. At other times, the lute appears stately and dignified, resplendent in a magnificent, proud set of robes. But the sparse arrangement, as well as the concentrated focus on one instrument, ensures that beneath the robed appearance there lies a body that’s thin bordering on the anorexic or even the skeletal, despite a flurry of faster passages that seem to run at quite a pace and with a good deal of urgency. The notes are still as narrow as a spindle, and that’s just a characteristic of the lute. Pockets of light are able to shine weakly out from the brighter tracks, offering a pale, stained-glass-window light. There are other reinterpretations of death here, too: a death of a nation as the British PM makes a suicidal statement. But the rose is still beautiful even as it dies. The future has and always will be an uncertain unknown, but willingly jumping off the edge without first looking down or checking to see where you’re going seems to be neither a sane nor reasonable course of action. Nobody Living Can Ever Make Me Turn Back revels in its uncertainty and in its transient nature. It began as dust, and to dust it returns. www.consouling.be
items._genre: early music / dark folk / lute / experimental folk
items._cn_summary: Jozef Van Wissem以鲁特琴为核心媒介，将中世纪音乐的纤细旋律转化为当代声音景观。专辑封面取材自比利时画家Cindy Wright的画作，整体概念围绕死亡、衰败与短暂性展开。乐评运用大量文学化比喻，将音乐比作中世纪欧洲城镇中蔓延的黑死病、教堂彩窗的幽光与古老土壤的厚重。编曲极度稀疏，单一鲁特琴在空旷声场中延展，偶尔加入爆炸性节拍冲击中世纪质感。声音时而庄严华贵，时而枯瘦如骷髅，体现出乐手在演奏中游走于快感与痛感之间的张力。专辑也暗含对当代政治的影射，以自杀式的政治表态呼应死亡的多种诠释。整体气质沉郁、神秘且充满仪式感。
